about.title: American Canyon Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: American Canyon's mix of logistics, warehousing, and light industrial work along corridors like Broadway and Flosden Road brings its share of on-the-job injuries. When a work accident happens, California generally routes injured employees through the workers' compensation system rather than a lawsuit against the employer. But that's not always the end of the story. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver on a road like Rt 29 contributed to the accident, a separate claim against that third party may be possible alongside workers' comp. Sorting out which path applies, or whether both do, takes a careful look at how the injury actually happened. We review the details of workplace accidents and explain the realistic options available to you.

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: California law generally treats workers' comp as the exclusive remedy against an employer, but a negligent third party, like a subcontractor or equipment maker, can still be pursued separately.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter Early On
items.desc: Workplace injuries generally need to be reported to an employer within 30 days, and missing that window can complicate a claim before it even starts.

items.title: Retaliation Is Against the Law
items.desc: California law prohibits employer retaliation against workers for reporting an injury or filing a claim, and we can help explain what protections apply.

items.question: I was hurt on a jobsite near Rt 29 — is workers' comp my only option?
items.answer: Usually workers' comp is the main path when an employer is involved, since California treats it as the exclusive remedy in most cases. However, if a third party, like a driver, contractor, or equipment supplier, contributed to your injury, you may also have a separate claim against them. We can review the specifics of what happened and explain which routes apply.

items.question: How long do I have to report my injury to my employer?
items.answer: California generally requires injured workers to report a workplace injury to their employer within 30 days. Waiting longer can make it harder to establish that the injury happened on the job. If you're unsure whether you're still within that window, it's worth getting guidance quickly.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: No, California law makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against a worker for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If you believe you've faced retaliation after an injury near your American Canyon workplace, we can help you understand your options.
